Powers and roots

Product

am an=am+na^m\,a^n = a^{m+n}aman=am+n

The idea

ama^mam is mmm factors aaa, ana^nan is nnn more; together m+nm + nm+n factors. The rule needs the same base: 23⋅322^3\cdot 3^223⋅32 cannot be combined this way. On the board: three blue factors and two yellow ones line up into five.

Worked example

23⋅24=27=1282^3\cdot 2^4 = 2^7 = 12823⋅24=27=128; x2⋅x5=x7x^2\cdot x^5 = x^7x2⋅x5=x7.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Quotient

aman=am−n\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}anam​=am−n

The idea

Dividing cancels nnn of the mmm factors, so m−nm - nm−n remain. If n>mn > mn>m the exponent is negative, which simply means the factors are left in the denominator. On the board: each factor below cancels one above; three are left.

Worked example

5754=53=125\tfrac{5^7}{5^4} = 5^3 = 1255457​=53=125; x2x5=x−3=1x3\tfrac{x^2}{x^5} = x^{-3} = \tfrac{1}{x^3}x5x2​=x−3=x31​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Power of a power

(am)n=amn\left(a^m\right)^n = a^{mn}(am)n=amn

The idea

(am)n\left(a^m\right)^n(am)n is nnn blocks of mmm factors each: mnmnmn factors. Do not confuse with amna^{m^n}amn, which means a(mn)a^{(m^n)}a(mn). On the board: n rows of m factors make m·n factors.

Worked example

(23)2=26=64\left(2^3\right)^2 = 2^6 = 64(23)2=26=64, while 232=29=5122^{3^2} = 2^9 = 512232=29=512.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Power of a product

(ab)n=anbn(ab)^n = a^n b^n(ab)n=anbn(ab)n=anbn\left(\frac ab\right)^n = \frac{a^n}{b^n}(ba​)n=bnan​

The idea

(ab)n(ab)^n(ab)n is nnn copies of ababab; reorder them as nnn copies of aaa times nnn copies of bbb. The exponent goes to every factor — but not to the terms of a sum: (a+b)2≠a2+b2(a + b)^2 \ne a^2 + b^2(a+b)2=a2+b2. On the board: each column is one factor ab; read the rows instead and you get aⁿ and bⁿ.

Worked example

(3x)2=9x2(3x)^2 = 9x^2(3x)2=9x2; (23)3=827\left(\tfrac23\right)^3 = \tfrac{8}{27}(32​)3=278​.

Negative and zero exponents

a−n=1ana^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}a−n=an1​a0=1 (a≠0)a^0 = 1 \ (a \ne 0)a0=1 (a=0)

The idea

Keep dividing by aaa: a3,a2,a1a^3, a^2, a^1a3,a2,a1, then a0=1a^0 = 1a0=1, a−1=1aa^{-1} = \tfrac1aa−1=a1​, a−2=1a2a^{-2} = \tfrac{1}{a^2}a−2=a21​. The definitions are exactly what keeps the quotient rule working.

Worked example

2−3=182^{-3} = \tfrac182−3=81​; (23)−2=94\left(\tfrac23\right)^{-2} = \tfrac94(32​)−2=49​; 70=17^0 = 170=1.

Fractional exponents

am/n=amn=(an)ma^{m/n} = \sqrt[n]{a^m} = \left(\sqrt[n]{a}\right)^mam/n=nam​=(na​)m

The idea

a1/na^{1/n}a1/n is the number whose nnn-th power is aaa: the nnn-th root. Then am/na^{m/n}am/n is that root raised to the power mmm. Take the root first — the numbers stay small. On the graph: x1/2=sqrtxx^{1/2} = sqrt xx1/2=sqrtx undoes x2x^2x2 — the two curves are mirror images in y=xy = xy=x.

Worked example

82/3=(83)2=22=48^{2/3} = \left(\sqrt[3]8\right)^2 = 2^2 = 482/3=(38​)2=22=4; 274/3=34=8127^{4/3} = 3^4 = 81274/3=34=81.

Roots

ab=a b\sqrt{ab} = \sqrt a\,\sqrt bab​=a​b​ab=ab\sqrt{\frac ab} = \frac{\sqrt a}{\sqrt b}ba​​=b​a​​

For a,b≥0a, b \ge 0a,b≥0.

The idea

Roots of products split into products of roots. To simplify, pull out the largest square factor: 50=25⋅2=52\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25\cdot 2} = 5\sqrt250​=25⋅2​=52​. Sums do not split: 9+16=5\sqrt{9 + 16} = 59+16​=5, not 777. On the board: an area of 4cdot9=364cdot 9 = 364cdot9=36 made of nine squares of area 4 — its side is sqrt4cdotsqrt9=2cdot3sqrt4cdotsqrt9 = 2cdot 3sqrt4cdotsqrt9=2cdot3.

Worked example

72=36⋅2=62\sqrt{72} = \sqrt{36\cdot 2} = 6\sqrt272​=36⋅2​=62​; 925=35\sqrt{\tfrac{9}{25}} = \tfrac35259​​=53​.

Rationalising

1a+b=a−ba−b\frac{1}{\sqrt a + \sqrt b} = \frac{\sqrt a - \sqrt b}{a - b}a​+b​1​=a−ba​−b​​

The idea

Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate a−b\sqrt a - \sqrt ba​−b​: the denominator becomes a difference of squares, a−ba - ba−b, with no roots left.

Worked example

13+2=3−23−2=3−2\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3 + \sqrt2} = \tfrac{\sqrt3 - \sqrt2}{3 - 2} = \sqrt3 - \sqrt23​+2​1​=3−23​−2​​=3​−2​; 63=633=23\tfrac{6}{\sqrt3} = \tfrac{6\sqrt3}{3} = 2\sqrt33​6​=363​​=23​.

Square root of a square

x2=∣x∣\sqrt{x^2} = |x|x2​=∣x∣

The idea

 \sqrt{\ } ​ always gives the non-negative root, so x2\sqrt{x^2}x2​ is xxx only when x≥0x \ge 0x≥0; for negative xxx it is −x-x−x. In one formula: ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣. Forgetting this loses solutions or creates false ones.

Worked example

(−3)2=9=3=∣−3∣\sqrt{(-3)^2} = \sqrt9 = 3 = \lvert -3\rvert(−3)2​=9​=3=∣−3∣; (x−2)2=∣x−2∣\sqrt{(x - 2)^2} = \lvert x - 2\rvert(x−2)2​=∣x−2∣.

Logarithms

Definition

log⁡ax=y  ⟺  ay=x\log_a x = y \iff a^y = xloga​x=y⟺ay=x(a>0, a≠1, x>0)(a > 0,\ a \ne 1,\ x > 0)(a>0, a=1, x>0)

Symbols: aaa: the base, xxx: the argument, yyy: the exponent you are looking for.

The idea

log⁡ax\log_a xloga​x answers “which power of aaa gives xxx?”. It is the inverse of x↦axx \mapsto a^xx↦ax, so it only accepts x>0x > 0x>0, and the base must be positive and not 1.

Worked example

log⁡232=5\log_2 32 = 5log2​32=5 because 25=322^5 = 3225=32; log⁡319=−2\log_3\tfrac19 = -2log3​91​=−2 because 3−2=193^{-2} = \tfrac193−2=91​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Product and quotient

log⁡(xy)=log⁡x+log⁡y\log(xy) = \log x + \log ylog(xy)=logx+logylog⁡xy=log⁡x−log⁡y\log\frac xy = \log x - \log ylogyx​=logx−logy

Symbols: log⁡\loglog without a base means the same base everywhere (often 10). The rules hold for any base.

The idea

Multiplying numbers adds their exponents, so logs turn products into sums and quotients into differences. Use it both ways: to expand, or to combine several logs into one. On the graph of lnxln xlnx: the height at 6 is the height at 2 stacked on the height at 3.

Worked example

log⁡2+log⁡50=log⁡100=2\log 2 + \log 50 = \log 100 = 2log2+log50=log100=2 (base 10) — no calculator needed.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Power

log⁡xk=klog⁡x\log x^k = k\log xlogxk=klogx

The idea

xkx^kxk is kkk factors xxx, so its log is kkk copies of log⁡x\log xlogx. This brings exponents down — the key step for solving ax=ba^x = bax=b. On the graph of log2xlog_2 xlog2​x: squaring or cubing xxx doubles or triples the height.

Worked example

log⁡8=3log⁡2\log 8 = 3\log 2log8=3log2; log⁡33=12\log_3\sqrt3 = \tfrac12log3​3​=21​.

Change of base

log⁡ax=ln⁡xln⁡a=log⁡bxlog⁡ba\log_a x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln a} = \frac{\log_b x}{\log_b a}loga​x=lnalnx​=logb​alogb​x​

Symbols: ln⁡\lnln is the natural logarithm, base e≈2.718e \approx 2.718e≈2.718; bbb is any other base.

The idea

Calculators know ln⁡\lnln and log⁡10\log_{10}log10​; any other base is a ratio of two of those. Choose a common base that makes both numbers nice powers. On the graph: every logarithm is the same curve stretched vertically by a constant factor frac1lna frac{1}{ln a}frac1lna.

Worked example

log⁡48=log⁡28log⁡24=32\log_4 8 = \tfrac{\log_2 8}{\log_2 4} = \tfrac32log4​8=log2​4log2​8​=23​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Inverse of the power

alog⁡ax=xa^{\log_a x} = xaloga​x=xlog⁡aax=x\log_a a^x = xloga​ax=x

The idea

log⁡a\log_aloga​ and a( )a^{(\ )}a( ) are inverse functions: one undoes the other. Use it to simplify towers like 102log⁡310^{2\log 3}102log3: first move the 2 inside, 10log⁡9=910^{\log 9} = 910log9=9. On the graph: 2x2^x2x and log2xlog_2 xlog2​x swap xxx and yyy, so each undoes the other — mirror images in y=xy = xy=x.

Worked example

3log⁡37=73^{\log_3 7} = 73log3​7=7; log⁡225=5\log_2 2^5 = 5log2​25=5; eln⁡4=4e^{\ln 4} = 4eln4=4.

Special values

log⁡a1=0,log⁡aa=1,ln⁡e=1\log_a 1 = 0, \quad \log_a a = 1, \quad \ln e = 1loga​1=0,loga​a=1,lne=1

Symbols: e≈2.718e \approx 2.718e≈2.718 is Euler’s number, the base of ln⁡\lnln.

The idea

Every base gives a0=1a^0 = 1a0=1 and a1=aa^1 = aa1=a, so log⁡a1=0\log_a 1 = 0loga​1=0 and log⁡aa=1\log_a a = 1loga​a=1. On the graph, every log⁡a\log_aloga​ crosses the xxx-axis at (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0).

Worked example

log⁡51+log⁡55=0+1=1\log_5 1 + \log_5 5 = 0 + 1 = 1log5​1+log5​5=0+1=1; ln⁡e3=3\ln e^3 = 3lne3=3.

Swap base and argument

log⁡ab=1log⁡ba\log_a b = \frac{1}{\log_b a}loga​b=logb​a1​

The idea

By change of base, log⁡ab=ln⁡bln⁡a\log_a b = \tfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}loga​b=lnalnb​ and log⁡ba=ln⁡aln⁡b\log_b a = \tfrac{\ln a}{\ln b}logb​a=lnblna​: they are reciprocals. So their product is always 1.

Worked example

log⁡82=1log⁡28=13\log_8 2 = \tfrac{1}{\log_2 8} = \tfrac13log8​2=log2​81​=31​; log⁡23⋅log⁡32=1\log_2 3\cdot\log_3 2 = 1log2​3⋅log3​2=1.

Identities

Square of a sum

(a±b)2=a2±2ab+b2(a \pm b)^2 = a^2 \pm 2ab + b^2(a±b)2=a2±2ab+b2

The idea

Picture a square of side a+ba + ba+b: it splits into a2a^2a2, b2b^2b2 and two ababab rectangles. The middle term 2ab2ab2ab is the one people forget. On the board: the square of side a+ba + ba+b is one a2a^2a2, one b2b^2b2 and two yellow ababab strips.

Worked example

1032=(100+3)2=10 000+600+9=10 609103^2 = (100 + 3)^2 = 10\,000 + 600 + 9 = 10\,6091032=(100+3)2=10000+600+9=10609.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Difference of squares

a2−b2=(a−b)(a+b)a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)a2−b2=(a−b)(a+b)

The idea

(a−b)(a+b)(a - b)(a + b)(a−b)(a+b): the cross terms +ab+ab+ab and −ab-ab−ab cancel. Read backwards, it factors any difference of two squares — and gives quick mental products. On the board: take the square a2a^2a2, cut away b2b^2b2, then move the yellow strip — the L-shape becomes a rectangle (a+b)(a−b)(a + b)(a - b)(a+b)(a−b).

Worked example

47⋅53=(50−3)(50+3)=2500−9=249147\cdot 53 = (50 - 3)(50 + 3) = 2500 - 9 = 249147⋅53=(50−3)(50+3)=2500−9=2491; x2−9=(x−3)(x+3)x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3)x2−9=(x−3)(x+3).

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Cube of a sum

(a±b)3=a3±3a2b+3ab2±b3(a \pm b)^3 = a^3 \pm 3a^2b + 3ab^2 \pm b^3(a±b)3=a3±3a2b+3ab2±b3

The idea

The coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1 are row 3 of Pascal’s triangle. With a minus sign, the signs alternate: +,−,+,−+, -, +, -+,−,+,−. On the board: the cube of side a+ba + ba+b pulled apart — one a3a^3a3 (blue), three a2ba^2ba2b (yellow), three ab2ab^2ab2 (green), one b3b^3b3 (pink). Drag it to turn it.

Worked example

(x+2)3=x3+6x2+12x+8(x + 2)^3 = x^3 + 6x^2 + 12x + 8(x+2)3=x3+6x2+12x+8.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Sum and difference of cubes

a3±b3=(a±b)(a2∓ab+b2)a^3 \pm b^3 = (a \pm b)\left(a^2 \mp ab + b^2\right)a3±b3=(a±b)(a2∓ab+b2)

The idea

a3+b3a^3 + b^3a3+b3 always has the factor a+ba + ba+b, and a3−b3a^3 - b^3a3−b3 the factor a−ba - ba−b; the other factor is a2∓ab+b2a^2 \mp ab + b^2a2∓ab+b2 (signs opposite to the first). It also gives a3+b3=(a+b)3−3ab(a+b)a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)^3 - 3ab(a + b)a3+b3=(a+b)3−3ab(a+b). On the board: a cube a3a^3a3 with the small cube b3b^3b3 (dashed) removed falls into three boxes, all with one side a−ba - ba−b: a2a^2a2, ababab and b2b^2b2 times (a−b)(a - b)(a−b).

Worked example

x3−8=(x−2)(x2+2x+4)x^3 - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)x3−8=(x−2)(x2+2x+4); 27+y3=(3+y)(9−3y+y2)27 + y^3 = (3 + y)(9 - 3y + y^2)27+y3=(3+y)(9−3y+y2).

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Three terms

(a+b+c)2=a2+b2+c2+2(ab+bc+ca)(a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + 2(ab + bc + ca)(a+b+c)2=a2+b2+c2+2(ab+bc+ca)

The idea

Each term squared, plus twice every product of two different terms. Rearranged, it links the sum, the sum of squares and the sum of pairwise products: knowing two gives the third. On the board: the square of side a+b+ca + b + ca+b+c — three squares on the diagonal, and each product ab,bc,caab, bc, caab,bc,ca appears twice.

Worked example

a+b+c=6a + b + c = 6a+b+c=6, ab+bc+ca=11ab + bc + ca = 11ab+bc+ca=11: a2+b2+c2=36−22=14a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 36 - 22 = 14a2+b2+c2=36−22=14 (e.g. 1, 2, 3).

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Difference of powers

an−bn=(a−b)(an−1+an−2b+⋯+bn−1)a^n - b^n = (a - b)\left(a^{n-1} + a^{n-2}b + \dots + b^{n-1}\right)an−bn=(a−b)(an−1+an−2b+⋯+bn−1)

The idea

a−ba - ba−b always divides an−bna^n - b^nan−bn; the other factor is the geometric sum an−1+an−2b+⋯+bn−1a^{n-1} + a^{n-2}b + \dots + b^{n-1}an−1+an−2b+⋯+bn−1. With b=1b = 1b=1: xn−1=(x−1)(xn−1+⋯+x+1)x^n - 1 = (x - 1)(x^{n-1} + \dots + x + 1)xn−1=(x−1)(xn−1+⋯+x+1).

Worked example

x4−1=(x−1)(x3+x2+x+1)x^4 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^3 + x^2 + x + 1)x4−1=(x−1)(x3+x2+x+1); 75−257^5 - 2^575−25 is divisible by 555.

Quadratic equations

Roots of ax² + bx + c = 0

x=−b±b2−4ac2ax = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​

Symbols: aaa, bbb, ccc: the coefficients of ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0 (a≠0a \ne 0a=0); ±\pm± gives the two roots.

The idea

Completing the square in ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0 gives the formula. The roots are where the parabola meets the xxx-axis, symmetric about x=−b2ax = -\tfrac{b}{2a}x=−2ab​.

Worked example

2x2+3x−2=02x^2 + 3x - 2 = 02x2+3x−2=0: Δ=9+16=25\Delta = 9 + 16 = 25Δ=9+16=25, x=−3±54x = \tfrac{-3 \pm 5}{4}x=4−3±5​, so x=12x = \tfrac12x=21​ or x=−2x = -2x=−2.

Discriminant

Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac

Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0: two real roots; Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0: one double root; Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0: two complex roots.

Symbols: Δ\DeltaΔ (delta): the discriminant, the number under the square root of the formula.

The idea

Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac is what sits under the root. Positive: two real roots (the parabola crosses the axis). Zero: one double root (it touches). Negative: no real roots (it stays on one side).

Worked example

x2+4x+5x^2 + 4x + 5x2+4x+5: Δ=16−20=−4<0\Delta = 16 - 20 = -4 < 0Δ=16−20=−4<0, no real roots. x2−6x+9x^2 - 6x + 9x2−6x+9: Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0, double root 3.

Vieta’s formulas

x1+x2=−bax_1 + x_2 = -\frac bax1​+x2​=−ab​x1x2=cax_1 x_2 = \frac cax1​x2​=ac​

Symbols: x1x_1x1​, x2x_2x2​: the two roots of ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0.

The idea

Expand a(x−x1)(x−x2)a(x - x_1)(x - x_2)a(x−x1​)(x−x2​) and compare with ax2+bx+cax^2 + bx + cax2+bx+c: the sum of the roots is −ba-\tfrac ba−ab​ and the product ca\tfrac caac​. They let you work with the roots without finding them. On the graph of x2−5x+4x^2 - 5x + 4x2−5x+4: the roots 1 and 4 add up to 5 =−fracba= - frac ba=−fracba and multiply to 4 =fracca= frac ca=fracca, the height where the curve meets the yyy-axis.

Worked example

x2−7x+10x^2 - 7x + 10x2−7x+10: sum 7, product 10 — the roots are 2 and 5. And x12+x22=(x1+x2)2−2x1x2x_1^2 + x_2^2 = (x_1 + x_2)^2 - 2x_1x_2x12​+x22​=(x1​+x2​)2−2x1​x2​.

Vertex form

ax2+bx+c=a(x+b2a)2−Δ4aax^2 + bx + c = a\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{\Delta}{4a}ax2+bx+c=a(x+2ab​)2−4aΔ​

Vertex at x=−b2ax = -\tfrac{b}{2a}x=−2ab​.

The idea

Complete the square: ax2+bx+c=a(x+b2a)2−Δ4aax^2 + bx + c = a\left(x + \tfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \tfrac{\Delta}{4a}ax2+bx+c=a(x+2ab​)2−4aΔ​. The vertex is (−b2a,−Δ4a)\left(-\tfrac{b}{2a}, -\tfrac{\Delta}{4a}\right)(−2ab​,−4aΔ​), which gives the minimum (if a>0a > 0a>0) or maximum value.

Worked example

2x2−8x+3=2(x2−4x+4)−8+3=2(x−2)2−52x^2 - 8x + 3 = 2(x^2 - 4x + 4) - 8 + 3 = 2(x - 2)^2 - 52x2−8x+3=2(x2−4x+4)−8+3=2(x−2)2−5: minimum −5-5−5 at x=2x = 2x=2.

Factored form

ax2+bx+c=a(x−x1)(x−x2)ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - x_1)(x - x_2)ax2+bx+c=a(x−x1​)(x−x2​)

Symbols: x1x_1x1​, x2x_2x2​: the roots; aaa: the leading coefficient.

The idea

If x1x_1x1​, x2x_2x2​ are the roots, the quadratic is a(x−x1)(x−x2)a(x - x_1)(x - x_2)a(x−x1​)(x−x2​). To factor, find the roots (formula or Vieta) and write them in. Don’t forget the leading coefficient aaa. On the graph: the factors are zero at the roots; aaa only stretches the parabola (dashed: a=1a = 1a=1, yellow: a=2a = 2a=2) — the roots stay put.

Worked example

2x2−x−32x^2 - x - 32x2−x−3: roots 32\tfrac3223​ and −1-1−1, so 2(x−32)(x+1)=(2x−3)(x+1)2\left(x - \tfrac32\right)(x + 1) = (2x - 3)(x + 1)2(x−23​)(x+1)=(2x−3)(x+1).

Polynomials

Remainder theorem

P(x)=(x−a) Q(x)+P(a)P(x) = (x - a)\,Q(x) + P(a)P(x)=(x−a)Q(x)+P(a)

The remainder of P(x)P(x)P(x) divided by x−ax - ax−a is P(a)P(a)P(a).

Symbols: P(x)P(x)P(x): the polynomial, Q(x)Q(x)Q(x): the quotient of the division.

The idea

Dividing by x−ax - ax−a leaves a constant remainder rrr: P(x)=(x−a)Q(x)+rP(x) = (x - a)Q(x) + rP(x)=(x−a)Q(x)+r. Put x=ax = ax=a: the first term vanishes, so r=P(a)r = P(a)r=P(a). No long division needed. On the graph: the remainder of dividing by x−2x - 2x−2 is just the height P(2)P(2)P(2).

A remainder of 0 means x−ax - ax−a divides PPP. So every root gives a factor, and finding one root of a cubic reduces it to a quadratic.

On the graph of 4x−5cdot2x+44^x - 5cdot 2^x + 44x−5cdot2x+4: with t=2xt = 2^xt=2x it is (t−1)(t−4)(t - 1)(t - 4)(t−1)(t−4), zero at t=1,4t = 1, 4t=1,4, that is x=0x = 0x=0 and x=2x = 2x=2.

Worked example

4x−6⋅2x+8=04^x - 6\cdot 2^x + 8 = 04x−6⋅2x+8=0: t2−6t+8=0t^2 - 6t + 8 = 0t2−6t+8=0, t=2t = 2t=2 or 444, so x=1x = 1x=1 or x=2x = 2x=2.

Logarithmic equations

log⁡af=log⁡ag  ⟺  f=g>0\log_a f = \log_a g \iff f = g > 0loga​f=loga​g⟺f=g>0log⁡af=c  ⟺  f=ac\log_a f = c \iff f = a^cloga​f=c⟺f=ac

Always check the solutions in the original domain (arguments > 0).

The idea

Combine everything into a single log, then either compare arguments (log⁡f=log⁡g\log f = \log glogf=logg) or rewrite as a power (log⁡af=c  ⟺  f=ac\log_a f = c \iff f = a^cloga​f=c⟺f=ac). Always check that the original arguments are positive — that removes false roots. On the graph of log2x+log2(x−2)log_2 x + log_2(x - 2)log2​x+log2​(x−2): it only exists for x>2x > 2x>2 (dashed wall), and it reaches 3 at x=4x = 4x=4; the algebraic root x=−2x = -2x=−2 is outside and must be rejected.

Worked example

log⁡x+log⁡(x−3)=1\log x + \log(x - 3) = 1logx+log(x−3)=1: x(x−3)=10x(x - 3) = 10x(x−3)=10, so x=5x = 5x=5 or x=−2x = -2x=−2. Only x=5x = 5x=5 keeps both arguments positive.

Inequalities and the base

0<a<1:  af<ag  ⟺  f>g0 < a < 1:\ \ a^f < a^g \iff f > g0<a<1:  af<ag⟺f>glog⁡af<log⁡ag  ⟺  f>g>0\log_a f < \log_a g \iff f > g > 0loga​f<loga​g⟺f>g>0

With a base between 0 and 1 the inequality sign flips.

The idea

If a>1a > 1a>1, axa^xax and log⁡ax\log_a xloga​x are increasing: the inequality keeps its direction. If 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1 they are decreasing: the direction flips. For logs, also require the arguments to be positive.

Worked example

(12)x>18=(12)3\left(\tfrac12\right)^x > \tfrac18 = \left(\tfrac12\right)^3(21​)x>81​=(21​)3: the base is less than 1, so x<3x < 3x<3.

Irrational equations

f=g  ⟺  f=g2,  g≥0\sqrt{f} = g \iff f = g^2,\ \ g \ge 0f​=g⟺f=g2,  g≥0

Isolate the root and square; squaring can add false solutions, so check every one.

The idea

Isolate the root and square. Squaring can create false solutions (it turns g=−fg = -\sqrt fg=−f​ into a solution too), so keep only those with g≥0g \ge 0g≥0 — or check every answer in the original equation.

a1=S1a_1 = S_1a1​=S1​an=Sn−Sn−1(n≥2)a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \quad (n \ge 2)an​=Sn​−Sn−1​(n≥2)

The idea

SnS_nSn​ is the sum up to term nnn, so the nnn-th term is what SnS_nSn​ adds to Sn−1S_{n-1}Sn−1​. This only works for n≥2n \ge 2n≥2; check n=1n = 1n=1 separately with a1=S1a_1 = S_1a1​=S1​. Arithmetic and geometric means

a,b,c (A)  ⟺  2b=a+ca, b, c\ (\text{A}) \iff 2b = a + ca,b,c (A)⟺2b=a+ca,b,c (G)  ⟺  b2=aca, b, c\ (\text{G}) \iff b^2 = aca,b,c (G)⟺b2=ac

A: arithmetic, G: geometric.

The idea

Three numbers form an arithmetic sequence when the middle one is the average of its neighbours, and a geometric one when its square is their product. Use this to turn “these are in progression” into an equation. On the board: in an arithmetic sequence the middle term sits halfway (2, 6, 10); in a geometric one it is the same factor up and down (1, 2, 4).

Worked example

Between 3 and 27: the arithmetic mean is 15, the geometric mean is 9 (3, 9, 27 with ratio 3).

Index properties

m+n=p+q ⇒ am+an=ap+aq  (A)m + n = p + q \ \Rightarrow\ a_m + a_n = a_p + a_q \ \ (\text{A})m+n=p+q ⇒ am​+an​=ap​+aq​  (A)aman=apaq  (G)a_m a_n = a_p a_q \ \ (\text{G})am​an​=ap​aq​  (G)

Symbols: A: arithmetic sequence, G: geometric sequence; m,n,p,qm, n, p, qm,n,p,q are positions (indices).

The idea

In an arithmetic sequence terms equally far from a centre add up to the same value; in a geometric one they multiply to the same value. So if m+n=p+qm + n = p + qm+n=p+q, then am+an=ap+aqa_m + a_n = a_p + a_qam​+an​=ap​+aq​ (A) or aman=apaqa_ma_n = a_pa_qam​an​=ap​aq​ (G).

Worked example

Arithmetic with a3+a9=20a_3 + a_9 = 20a3​+a9​=20: since 3+9=6+63 + 9 = 6 + 63+9=6+6, 2a6=202a_6 = 202a6​=20, so a6=10a_6 = 10a6​=10 — without knowing a1a_1a1​ or ddd.

Linear recurrence

an+1=p an+q ⇒ an−λ=p n−1(a1−λ),λ=q1−pa_{n+1} = p\,a_n + q \ \Rightarrow\ a_n - \lambda = p^{\,n-1}(a_1 - \lambda), \quad \lambda = \frac{q}{1 - p}an+1​=pan​+q ⇒ an​−λ=pn−1(a1​−λ),λ=1−pq​

λ\lambdaλ is the fixed point; an−λa_n - \lambdaan​−λ is geometric.

The idea

For an+1=pan+qa_{n+1} = pa_n + qan+1​=pan​+q, find the fixed point λ\lambdaλ with λ=pλ+q\lambda = p\lambda + qλ=pλ+q. The distance to it, an−λa_n - \lambdaan​−λ, is multiplied by ppp each step — a geometric sequence. So an=λ+pn−1(a1−λ)a_n = \lambda + p^{n-1}(a_1 - \lambda)an​=λ+pn−1(a1​−λ).

a1=1a_1 = 1a1​=1, an+1=2an+1a_{n+1} = 2a_n + 1an+1​=2an​+1: λ=−1\lambda = -1λ=−1, so an+1=2n−1⋅2a_n + 1 = 2^{n-1}\cdot 2an​+1=2n−1⋅2, i.e. an=2n−1a_n = 2^n - 1an​=2n−1 (1, 3, 7, 15, …).

Arithmetic × geometric

S=∑k rk:  S−rS=∑rk−n rn+1S = \sum k\,r^k:\ \ S - rS = \sum r^k - n\,r^{n+1}S=∑krk:  S−rS=∑rk−nrn+1

For S=∑k rkS = \sum k\,r^kS=∑krk, write rSrSrS shifted one place under SSS and subtract: the coefficients become all 1, leaving a plain geometric sum minus the last term. Then divide by 1−r1 - r1−r.

Telescoping fractions

1k(k+d)=1d(1k−1k+d)\frac{1}{k(k + d)} = \frac1d\left(\frac1k - \frac{1}{k + d}\right)k(k+d)1​=d1​(k1​−k+d1​)

The idea

When the factors in the denominator differ by ddd, split 1k(k+d)\tfrac{1}{k(k + d)}k(k+d)1​ into 1d(1k−1k+d)\tfrac1d\left(\tfrac1k - \tfrac{1}{k + d}\right)d1​(k1​−k+d1​). Linear programming

The problem

max⁡/min⁡ z=ax+by:aix+biy≤ci\max/\min\ z = ax + by \quad :\quad a_ix + b_iy \le c_imax/min z=ax+by:ai​x+bi​y≤ci​

The constraints (inequalities) cut out a polygon: the feasible region.

Symbols: zzz: the objective function to maximise or minimise; aia_iai​, bib_ibi​, cic_ici​: the numbers of the iii-th constraint.

The idea

Maximise or minimise a linear objective z=ax+byz = ax + byz=ax+by over the region allowed by linear constraints. The region is a polygon, and the best value is always reached at one of its corners: list the vertices, evaluate zzz, pick the best.

Worked example

Maximise z=3x+2yz = 3x + 2yz=3x+2y with x+y≤4x + y \le 4x+y≤4, x≤3x \le 3x≤3, x,y≥0x, y \ge 0x,y≥0. Vertices (0,0),(3,0),(3,1),(0,4)(0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 1), (0, 4)(0,0),(3,0),(3,1),(0,4) give z=0,9,11,8z = 0, 9, 11, 8z=0,9,11,8: the maximum is 11 at (3,1)(3, 1)(3,1).

Half-planes

ax+by≤cax + by \le cax+by≤c

Draw the line ax+by=cax + by = cax+by=c, test a point such as (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) to pick the side.

The idea

A line ax+by=cax + by = cax+by=c splits the plane in two; ax+by≤cax + by \le cax+by≤c is one side. To find which, test a point not on the line — the origin is easiest: if it satisfies the inequality, shade its side.

Worked example

2x+3y≤122x + 3y \le 122x+3y≤12: at (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0), 0≤120 \le 120≤12 is true, so the region is the side of the line containing the origin.

Optimum at a vertex

z∗=max⁡Viz(Vi)z^{*} = \max_{V_i} z(V_i)z∗=Vi​max​z(Vi​)

Find the vertices (intersections of the boundary lines) and evaluate z at each.

Symbols: ViV_iVi​: the vertices of the feasible region, z∗z^*z∗: the optimal (best) value.

The idea

A linear function cannot have a peak in the middle of a polygon: moving in the right direction always improves it until you hit the boundary, and along an edge until you hit a corner. So it suffices to compare the vertices.

Worked example

Same region, minimise z=x−yz = x - yz=x−y: values 0,3,2,−40, 3, 2, -40,3,2,−4, so the minimum is −4-4−4 at (0,4)(0, 4)(0,4).

Level lines

ax+by=c,c↑ax + by = c , \quad c \uparrowax+by=c,c↑

Slide the line z = c across the region; the last point it touches is the optimum. A whole edge can be optimal if it is parallel to z.

The idea

Each value of zzz gives a line ax+by=zax + by = zax+by=z; all these lines are parallel with slope −ab-\tfrac ab−ba​. Slide the line in the direction where zzz grows: the last point of the region it touches is the optimum.

Worked example

For z=3x+2yz = 3x + 2yz=3x+2y the level lines have slope −32-\tfrac32−23​; pushing them outwards, the last corner reached is (3,1)(3, 1)(3,1) with z=11z = 11z=11.

Binomial theorem

Expansion

(a+b)n=∑k=0n(nk)an−kbk(a + b)^n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom nk a^{n-k} b^k(a+b)n=k=0∑n​(kn​)an−kbk

Symbols: (nk)=n!k! (n−k)!\binom nk = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}(kn​)=k!(n−k)!n!​: “nnn choose kkk”, the binomial coefficient.

The idea

In (a+b)n(a + b)^n(a+b)n, each term picks bbb from kkk of the nnn brackets and aaa from the rest, which can be done in (nk)\binom nk(kn​) ways. The coefficients are a row of Pascal’s triangle. On the board: Pascal’s triangle — each number is the sum of the two above it. Row 4 (yellow) gives a4+4a3b+6a2b2+4ab3+b4a^4 + 4a^3b + 6a^2b^2 + 4ab^3 + b^4a4+4a3b+6a2b2+4ab3+b4.

(x+1)4=x4+4x3+6x2+4x+1(x + 1)^4 = x^4 + 4x^3 + 6x^2 + 4x + 1(x+1)4=x4+4x3+6x2+4x+1.

Tk+1=(nk)an−kbkT_{k+1} = \binom nk a^{n-k} b^kTk+1​=(kn​)an−kbk

Symbols: Tk+1T_{k+1}Tk+1​: the (k+1)(k + 1)(k+1)-th term of the expansion, the one containing bkb^kbk.

To find a particular power of xxx, write the exponent of xxx in Tk+1T_{k+1}Tk+1​ as a function of kkk and solve for kkk. Sum of coefficients

∑k=0n(nk)=2n\sum_{k=0}^n \binom nk = 2^nk=0∑n​(kn​)=2n∑k=0n(−1)k(nk)=0\sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k\binom nk = 0k=0∑n​(−1)k(kn​)=0

The idea

Put x=1x = 1x=1 in a polynomial and you get the sum of its coefficients. For (a+b)n(a + b)^n(a+b)n with a=b=1a = b = 1a=b=1: 2n2^n2n; with a=1a = 1a=1, b=−1b = -1b=−1: 000, so the even-position and odd-position coefficients have equal sums. On the board: every row of Pascal’s triangle adds up to a power of 2 — that is (1+1)n(1 + 1)^n(1+1)n.
